headline: Shawnee National Forest Sandstone Access and Safety
reservation: Entry to the Garden of the Gods Recreation Area is free and does not require a permit. However, camping at Pharaoh Campground is first-come, first-served and fills early during peak autumn weekends. For groups over 75 people, a special use permit from the Shawnee National Forest office is required.

days.title: The Ancient Sea Bed

stops.name: Observation Trail
stops.detail: Walk the quarter-mile flagstone path to see Camel Rock and Anvil Rock, formations carved from 320-million-year-old sandstone.

stops.name: Garden of the Gods Wilderness
stops.detail: Navigate the rugged backpacker trails below the rim to experience the hardwood forests and hidden bluff views.

days.driving: Allow 40 minutes from gateway; conditions vary on winding forest roads
days.note: Sandstone can be extremely slippery when wet; wear boots with significant traction.

days.title: Historic Hollows and River Pirates

stops.name: Rim Rock National Recreation Trail
stops.detail: Hike the circular escarpment trail and descend through 'Fat Man's Squeeze' into a lush, shaded valley.

stops.name: Cave-in-Rock State Park
stops.detail: Explore the 55-foot-wide riverside cavern on the Ohio River, a historic hideout for 19th-century outlaws.

days.driving: Allow 1 hour for the loop; local roads are narrow
days.note: Cave-in-Rock is roughly 25 minutes south of the main Garden area.

days.title: Iron and Stone Heritage

stops.name: Illinois Iron Furnace
stops.detail: Visit the only remaining charcoal iron furnace in Illinois, a testament to the region's 19th-century industrial past.

stops.name: River to River Trail Access
stops.detail: Walk a short segment of this 160-mile trail that bisects the Shawnee National Forest.

days.note: Download topographical maps as trail markers in the wilderness area can be sparse.

intel.title: Recreation Area Crowds
intel.text: The main Observation Trail lot is small and frequently overflows by mid-morning on October weekends. Arrive before 8 AM or visit on a Tuesday/Wednesday to ensure a space.

intel.title: Shawnee Dead Zones
intel.text: Cellular reception is notably poor throughout the Shawnee National Forest interior. Do not rely on streaming GPS; use offline maps or printed forest service charts.

intel.title: Rural Gateway Stations
intel.text: Fuel up in Harrisburg or Equality before entering the forest; there are no services at the trailheads. Ensure you have adequate water as concessions are not available on-site.

intel.title: Optimal Foliage Windows
intel.text: Mid-to-late October typically offers peak colors, but this varies by annual rainfall. Spring wildflowers bloom in April, though trails are often muddier during this period.

intel.title: Rim Safety
intel.text: The Observation Trail features steep, unprotected drops; keep children close and stay on the designated stone paths. Wilderness trails may involve creek crossings depending on recent rainfall.

plan.arrival: Fly into Evansville or St. Louis; rent a vehicle and secure all groceries in Harrisburg before entering the National Forest area.
plan.vehicle: Standard cars are fine for main access roads; AWD is helpful for certain gravel forest service roads during wet weather.
plan.goldenHour: Camel Rock at sunrise for the best light on the iron-stained sandstone; morning mist is common in the valley.
